parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Posh Pets Spain (PPS) *is a pet hotel in the village of Alhaurin el Grande, Spain. It is run by Rachel Goutorbe, an animal enthusiast, and her team of four pet specialists. *PPS *offers overnight accommodation with room for seven dogs or cats, a pet grooming service and a shop selling pet products, such as dog coats and dog leads. Pet grooming involves washing, cutting and combing a pet’s coat.

State **one **reason why *PPS* motivates its employees.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any 1 from:
> 
> - To retain its skilled pet specialists, as losing staff from such a small team would significantly affect PPS's ability to care for animals and serve customers **[1 mark]**
> - To improve the quality of care provided to pets at PPS, encouraging customers to return and recommend the business to others **[1 mark]**
> - To increase the productivity of its team so that PPS can take on more grooming appointments and accommodate more dogs and cats **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept any other appropriate response in the context of PPS.
> 
> Marks are not awarded for a reason that is not in the context of PPS.
> 
> "State" requires a clear, brief point without further explanation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure your answer is linked to the context of PPS — a generic reason such as "to make employees work harder" without any reference to the business will not earn the mark. Use details from the extract, such as the small team size, the grooming service or the pet accommodation, to show the examiner you understand why motivation matters for this particular business.

**[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *TUI *is a holiday business that has over 100 years of experience. It offers customers a variety of holidays including staying in hotels, and river and ocean-going cruises. There are many extras that it offers to holiday makers including: car hire, extensions to the holiday and arranging day trips at all its holiday destinations.
> 
> The business is well known and flies its customers to over 180 destinations around the world, including Greece, Turkey and Spain. It has 1,600 travel agencies and 27 million customers. Holidays can be booked by visiting a travel agency or online.
> 
> *TUI *has holidays to meet the needs of all its customers: families, children, couples and those with disabilities.
> 
> *TUI *wants to maintain its reputation by continuing to provide quality holidays and experiences that customers will enjoy. This will encourage them to return to book future holidays with *TUI.*

Outline **one **reason why *TUI* offers employees working in its travel agencies a commission based on the number of holidays they sell.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid reason. Award a further 1 mark for development of the reason.
> 
> - Commission motivates *TUI's* travel agency employees to sell as many holidays as possible **[1 mark]**
> - As the more holidays they sell the more money they earn, which directly increases *TUI's* revenue and helps it serve its 27 million customers **[1 mark]**
> 
> OR
> 
> - Offering commission encourages *TUI's* travel agency staff to provide excellent customer service **[1 mark]**
> - As building good relationships with customers makes them more likely to book a holiday, increasing the employee's earnings and helping *TUI* maintain its reputation for quality experiences **[1 mark]**
> 
> OR
> 
> - Commission rewards *TUI's* highest-performing travel agency employees financially **[1 mark]**
> - Which helps the business retain its best salespeople across its 1,600 travel agencies and reduces the cost of repeatedly recruiting and training new staff **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> "Outline" requires a brief statement of the key point (1 mark) with some development or linked reasoning (1 mark).

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks you to "outline", make sure you do more than just state a point — you need to briefly develop or explain it. A good approach is to give your reason in one sentence and then add a second sentence that explains *why* or *how* it links back to the business. For example, state what commission does for the employee and then explain the benefit this brings to *TUI*. Many students lose the second mark by simply repeating the same point in different words rather than genuinely extending their answer.

**[2 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **of the factors in Herzberg’s motivational theory.
parts.solution_md:
Herzberg identified motivators as factors that genuinely increase an employee's job satisfaction and motivation** [1 mark]**, such as being given greater responsibility or receiving recognition for achieving good results **[1 mark]**, which encourages employees to work harder and perform better, benefiting both the individual and the business **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid factor in Herzberg's theory. 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the factor, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Herzberg identified hygiene factors as conditions that, if poor, cause employees to feel dissatisfied with their job **[1 mark]**, such as low pay, poor working conditions or ineffective management **[1 mark]**, meaning that while improving these factors removes dissatisfaction, it does not in itself motivate employees to work harder **[1 mark]**
> - Herzberg argued that achievement is a key motivator **[1 mark]**, as employees who feel a sense of accomplishment when completing a challenging task are more likely to remain engaged and committed to their work **[1 mark]**, which can lead to higher productivity and a reduced likelihood of staff leaving the business **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response
> 
> Answers that list three factors in Herzberg's theory with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.solution_md:
Motivating employees encourages them to provide a higher standard of customer service **[1 mark]**, which is essential for Premier Inn as a business that relies on guests returning to its hotels across the UK, UAE, India and Germany **[1 mark]**. Satisfied guests are more likely to rebook and recommend Premier Inn to others, helping the business to grow its customer base and maintain revenue across its 820 hotels **[1 mark]**

Motivating employees also reduces staff turnover **[1 mark]**, which is particularly valuable for a large business like Premier Inn that would face significant recruitment and training costs if large numbers of its hotel staff regularly left **[1 mark]**. Retaining experienced employees helps Premier Inn maintain consistent service standards across all of its hotels, supporting its plans to continue expanding into new countries **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying valid benefits of motivating employees for Premier Inn.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to Premier Inn's context.
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the impact on Premier Inn.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Motivated employees are more productive in their roles **[1 mark]**, meaning Premier Inn's hotels can operate more efficiently with guests receiving prompt and attentive service throughout their stay **[1 mark]**. This supports Premier Inn's aim of encouraging guests to return, directly contributing to the profitability of its 820 hotels **[1 mark]**
> - Motivated employees are less likely to be absent from work **[1 mark]**, which helps Premier Inn to maintain adequate staffing levels across its hotels and restaurants **[1 mark]**. Consistent staffing ensures that the quality of service guests receive is not affected by shortages, protecting Premier Inn's reputation as it expands into new markets **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers that list six benefits of motivation with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
>

Here, make sure you calculate the commission on one jumper first before multiplying by the number of jumpers sold. A common mistake is to forget to multiply by 12 and only give the commission for a single jumper.

> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the reasons to TBTS's context.

> - Motivated employees are more productive in their roles **[1 mark]**, helping TBTS to manage stock efficiently across its three Singapore stores and fulfil online orders promptly through its website **[1 mark]**. > - Motivated employees are better able to represent TBTS's values to customers **[1 mark]**, particularly at the high-profile Jewel Changi Airport location where the store is visible to a large number of international visitors **[1 mark]**. Enthusiastic staff who genuinely believe in the quality and environmental credentials of TBTS's toys are more likely to build customer loyalty and grow the business's reputation **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **reason why a business would pay its employees above the minimum wage.
parts.solution_md:
Paying above the minimum wage helps a business to attract skilled and talented employees **[1 mark]**, as candidates with specialist knowledge or experience are likely to have several job offers and will choose the employer offering the most competitive pay **[1 mark]**, meaning the business is more likely to recruit high-quality staff who can contribute effectively and help the business to grow **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid reason. 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the reason, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Paying above the minimum wage helps a business to retain its most experienced employees **[1 mark]**, as staff who feel well rewarded financially are less likely to leave and seek higher pay elsewhere **[1 mark]**, reducing the cost of repeatedly recruiting and training new employees and helping the business to maintain a skilled and consistent workforce **[1 mark]**
> - Paying above the minimum wage motivates employees to work harder and be more productive **[1 mark]**, as staff who feel fairly rewarded are more likely to be committed to their role and take pride in the quality of their work **[1 mark]**, which can improve the standard of the product or service the business provides and help it to remain competitive **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> Answers that list three reasons for paying above minimum wage with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

The name *LEGO *is an abbreviation of two Danish words, ‘leg godt’ which means ‘play well’. It is now one of the world’s largest manufacturers of toys with 15 factories and over 18,000 employees around the world.

Calculate the employee’s new salary. You are advised to show your working.
parts.solution_md:
**Method 1:**

$150  000 \times 0 . 045 = 6  750$ **[1 mark]**

$150  000 + 6  750 =$ **156 750 DKK** **[1 mark]**

**Method 2:**

$150  000 \times 1 . 045$ **[1 mark]**

$=$ **156 750 DKK** **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **of the needs in Maslow’s motivational theory.
parts.solution_md:
Maslow identified physiological needs as the most basic level of his hierarchy **[1 mark]**, which include the need for food, warmth and shelter that employees meet through the wages they earn from work **[1 mark]**, meaning that if a business does not pay its employees enough to meet these basic needs, they will be unable to focus on performing well in their role **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying a valid need in Maslow's theory. 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the need, for a maximum of 3 marks.
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Maslow identified social needs as an important motivating factor **[1 mark]**, suggesting that employees have a need to feel a sense of belonging and build positive relationships with their colleagues at work **[1 mark]**, meaning businesses can motivate staff by encouraging teamwork and creating a friendly working environment where employees feel part of a group **[1 mark]**
> - Maslow identified esteem needs as a higher-level motivating factor **[1 mark]**, which refers to an employee's need to feel recognised, respected and valued for their contribution to the business **[1 mark]**, meaning that managers who praise employees and acknowledge their achievements are more likely to have a motivated and confident workforce **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response.
> 
> Answers that list three factors in Maslow's theory with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark.
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Irsi Chocolatier* is a chocolate shop in Brussels, the capital city of Belgium. There are many other chocolate shops nearby. Opened in 1989 by the Corne family the business now has four directors and three employees. Florent Corne is the Managing Director with three other family members as Directors.* Irsi Chocolatier *opens from Tuesday till Saturday. The shop sells a variety of handmade chocolates and jelly fruit sweets. It delivers locally and has a website for information purposes only.

*Irsi Chocolatier* is a business with three loyal employees. As it expands it wants to ensure its current and new employees remain happy and motivated within the workplace.

Evaluate the impact of *Irsi Chocolatier* using financial methods of motivation on its employees. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
Financial methods of motivation include pay rises, bonuses and commission, which reward employees with increased earnings in return for their performance or loyalty** [K]**

Financial rewards such as bonuses could motivate Irsi's employees to produce higher quality handmade chocolates and deliver better customer service **[K]**, which is important for a business operating in a highly competitive area of Brussels with many other chocolate shops nearby **[Ap]**. This could help Irsi attract more customers and increase sales, supporting the business as it looks to expand **[An]**

However, Irsi is a small family business with only three employees and four directors **[Ap]**, meaning its financial resources are likely to be limited, and it may struggle to sustain meaningful pay rises or bonuses over the long term **[K][An]**. According to Herzberg's theory, pay is a hygiene factor rather than a true motivator **[K]**, suggesting that while financial rewards may prevent dissatisfaction, they may not be sufficient to keep Irsi's employees genuinely motivated **[An]**. Non-financial methods such as recognition, greater responsibility or flexible working may be more effective for a small, close-knit team** [E]**

Overall, financial methods of motivation can help Irsi retain its three loyal employees and attract new staff as the business expands** [Ap] [E]**. However, given the business's limited size and resources** [Ap]**, a combination of financial and non-financial methods is likely to be the most effective approach to keeping employees happy and motivated in the long term** [E]**

> - Financial rewards alone may not address all of Irsi's employees' needs → according to Maslow, employees also need social belonging and esteem → suggesting non-financial methods such as recognition and teamwork are equally important in a small family business environment
> - Paying above the minimum wage helps Irsi attract skilled chocolatiers in a competitive Brussels market → ensuring the quality of its handmade products is maintained → protecting the business's reputation and helping it stand out from nearby competitors

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *IKEA* is a well-known home furniture retailer with stores throughout the world. It was started in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad when he was given some money by his father for doing well at school. He wanted to produce furniture at a price that people could afford to buy.
> 
> He realised that transporting furniture to customers was difficult, as goods were often damaged. He developed flat packs to avoid damage. A flat pack contained all the materials needed to self-assemble a table, a chair or a bed.
> 
> All *IKEA *stores are run as franchises.

To motivate employees working in its factories, *IKEA *is considering two motivational methods.

- **Option 1**: bonus
- **Option 2**: job enrichment.

Justify which **one **of these two options *IKEA *should use.
parts.solution_md:
A bonus  is a financial reward paid to employees on top of their regular wage, while job enrichment involves giving employees more varied and challenging tasks to make their work more fulfilling** [K]**

One benefit of a bonus is that it directly rewards IKEA's factory workers for meeting production targets** [K]**, motivating them to work more efficiently and increase output of flat pack furniture for IKEA's stores worldwide** [Ap] [An]**

However, according to Herzberg, financial rewards such as bonuses are hygiene factors rather than true motivators **[K]**, meaning that once IKEA's factory workers **[Ap]** become accustomed to receiving a bonus they may begin to expect it as part of their regular pay, reducing its long-term motivational impact** [An]**

One benefit of job enrichment is that it gives IKEA's factory workers greater variety and responsibility in their roles** [K] **constructing flat pack furniture**, **which according to Maslow addresses higher-level esteem needs and increases employees' sense of achievement and commitment to the business** [An]**

However, IKEA's factories rely on standardised production processes to ensure the consistent quality of its flat pack furniture** [Ap]**, meaning job enrichment may be difficult to implement without disrupting these processes and risking a fall in production standards** [An]**

IKEA should choose the bonus option **[E]**. With factories supplying stores throughout the world **[Ap]**, IKEA needs its factory workers to maintain high and consistent levels of productivity. A bonus provides a clear and immediate financial incentive to meet production targets, making it a more practical and measurable motivational tool than job enrichment in a large-scale manufacturing environment **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - **9-mark ‘justify’ questions are marked using a level-of-response grid (L1 - L3)**
> - Examiners judge how well the response demonstrates:
> 
>   - Accurate knowledge of relevant business concepts and terminology
>   - Application of ideas to the case study throughout the answer
>   - Logical chains of reasoning explaining business impacts
>   - A clear judgement, providing justification for the choice made
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - A bonus scheme tied to production output motivates IKEA's factory workers to meet targets consistently → ensuring a reliable supply of flat pack furniture to stores worldwide → supporting IKEA's reputation for affordable, accessible products
> - Job enrichment could reduce the monotony of repetitive factory work at IKEA → increasing employee satisfaction and reducing staff turnover → saving the business the cost of recruiting and training replacement workers
> - Standardised flat pack production requires precision and consistency → making it difficult to enrich factory roles without affecting quality → suggesting a bonus is more compatible with IKEA's manufacturing processes
> - Herzberg's theory suggests that recognition and responsibility are stronger long-term motivators than financial rewards → meaning job enrichment could sustain motivation more effectively than a bonus over time → potentially making it the better choice for retaining experienced factory workers

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *NEXT *is a well-known clothing retailer that operates in 70 countries and employs over 43,000 employees. Since *NEXT *commenced trading it has introduced many other products to its range such as home interiors, flowers and a wedding list service.
> 
> In 1999 *NEXT* launched its own online shopping platform, enabling customers to purchase its products where ever they live. It continues to improve its customer service by introducing new initiatives such as next day delivery.
> 
> *NEXT *mainly uses its own factories for production. However, it does purchase some clothes such as ladies dresses from Turkish factories.
> 
> *NEXT *works hard to remain competitive with other retailers of similar products.

*NEXT *understands that some employees are motivated by non-financial methods and these may help with employee retention. To do this *NEXT *is considering the following two options:

- **Option 1:** job rotation
- **Option 2:** job enrichment

Justify which **one **of these two options *NEXT *should choose.
parts.solution_md:
Job rotation involves employees regularly moving between different roles within a business, while job enrichment gives employees greater responsibility and more challenging tasks within their existing role **[K]**

One benefit of job rotation is that it gives NEXT's employees experience of a wider variety of tasks across different areas of the business **[K]**, such as working in stores, factories or supporting the online platform **[Ap]**, reducing the monotony of repetitive work and helping to retain staff** [An]**

However, employees who frequently rotate between roles may not develop deep expertise in any one area **[K]**, which could reduce the quality of work in specialist departments such as NEXT's factories that produce clothing to a high and consistent standard** [Ap] [An]**

One benefit of job enrichment is that it increases employees' sense of achievement and responsibility within their role** [K] **which, according to Herzberg are true motivators that create long-term job satisfaction rather than simply preventing dissatisfaction **[An]**, helping NEXT to retain its 43,000 employees across 70 countries** [Ap]**

However, not all employees may welcome greater responsibility** [K]**, and in NEXT's factories enriching roles could be difficult to implement without disrupting the standardised production processes needed to maintain clothing quality** [Ap] [An]**

NEXT should choose job enrichment **[E]**. As a business operating across 70 countries with over 43,000 employees** [Ap]**, retaining skilled and experienced staff is essential to maintaining the quality of its products and customer service initiatives, such as next-day delivery **[An]**. Job enrichment addresses this by giving employees genuine fulfilment in their roles, making them more likely to stay with NEXT long-term than job rotation alone would achieve** [E]**

> **Alternative ways to answer**

> - Job rotation across NEXT's stores, factories and online operations gives employees a broader understanding of the business → increasing their versatility and value to NEXT → helping the business to manage staffing flexibly across its operations in 70 countries
> - Job enrichment gives NEXT's employees greater ownership of their work → increasing motivation and job satisfaction according to Herzberg's motivational theory → reducing staff turnover and the cost of recruiting and training replacements across a large global workforce
> - Frequent job rotation may reduce employees' ability to specialise in key areas such as online platform management → weakening the quality of NEXT's customer service initiatives such as next day delivery → making job enrichment a more focused and effective motivational strategy
> - Enriching roles in NEXT's factories by giving workers responsibility for quality checking → increases their sense of achievement → helping NEXT maintain the high production standards needed to remain competitive with other clothing retailers

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *Huawei *is a leading global provider of information and communications technology, infrastructure and smart devices. In March 2011, over one million of its C8500 smartphones were sold in China following its launch.
> 
> It now manufactures a wide variety of different products including *Huawei *smartphones, watches and tablets. In recent years *Huawei *has won many awards. In 2018 it was named the 68th most valuable brand by Best Global Brands. In 2019 it introduced a smartphone which had new photographic technology.

*Huawei *use a range of motivational methods to ensure its employees remain with them and do not leave. It has to make a decision on which of the following two options it will use. It is considering two methods:

- **Option 1: **financial motivation
- **Option 2:** non-financial motivation

Justify which **one **of these two options *Huawei *should choose.
parts.solution_md:
Financial motivation includes methods such as bonuses and pay rises that reward employees with increased earnings, while non-financial motivation includes methods such as job enrichment, recognition and promotion opportunities that improve job satisfaction without direct financial reward **[K]**

One benefit of financial motivation is that high salaries and bonuses help Huawei attract and retain the skilled engineers and designers it needs to develop innovative products **[K]**, such as the new photographic technology introduced in its 2019 smartphone** [Ap] [An]**

However, according to Herzberg, financial rewards are hygiene factors rather than true motivators** [K]**, meaning that once Huawei's skilled employees **[Ap] **become accustomed to high pay they may no longer feel motivated to perform at their best, limiting the long-term effectiveness of financial methods** [An]**

One benefit of non-financial motivation is that methods such as recognition and promotion opportunities address higher-level needs in Maslow's hierarchy **[K]**, giving Huawei's employees a sense of achievement and career progression that sustains long-term motivation and reduces the likelihood of staff leaving for competitors such as Samsung** [Ap] [An]**

However, non-financial methods alone may not be sufficient to retain top talent **[K]**, as skilled technology professionals are in high demand and rival businesses may offer significantly higher salaries to attract Huawei's most experienced employees** [Ap] [An]**

Huawei should choose non-financial motivation** [E]**. As the 68th most valuable global brand and winner of multiple industry awards **[Ap]**, Huawei can offer employees the unique opportunity to work on cutting-edge technology that is recognised worldwide **[An]**. According to Herzberg, motivators such as achievement and recognition are more effective at sustaining long-term commitment than financial rewards, making non-financial methods the stronger choice for retaining Huawei's highly skilled workforce** [E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *The Alternative Drum School (TADS) *was set up in the wealthy area of Cricklade, England in 2008 by Ollie Tanner who had a passion for and enjoyed drumming. Ollie invested all of his savings into the drumming school. He saw the potential of being located away from other drumming schools.
> 
> Ollie promotes his business by writing columns in local papers, performing at local music festivals and by word of mouth recommendations. He has invested heavily in computer technology to allow students to produce the music they enjoy playing.
> 
> Ollie finds it difficult to maintain a good work-life balance. Ollie currently works 60 hours a week in a business that does not have reliable profits.

*TADS *currently pays its music teachers an hourly rate for every lesson they teach. It is looking to retain the teachers it currently employs.

It is considering the following two options:

- **Option 1: **commission for each new pupil taught
- **Option 2:** an increase in the hourly rate.

Justify which **one **of these two options *TADS *should use.
parts.solution_md:
Commission is a financial reward paid to employees based on their individual performance, while an increase in hourly rate raises the amount paid to employees for every hour they work** [K]**

One benefit of offering commission is that it incentivises TADS's teachers to actively recruit new pupils **[K]**, which could help grow the school's student base and generate more reliable income for a business with inconsistent profits** [Ap] [An]**

However, teachers who already have a full timetable of lessons may be unable to recruit new pupils and would therefore receive no benefit from commission **[K]**, meaning this option does not directly address TADS's goal of retaining all of its current teachers** [Ap] [An]**

One benefit of increasing the hourly rate is that it immediately improves the earnings of all of TADS's teachers **[K]**, making them feel more valued and financially rewarded for the lessons they teach, increasing the likelihood they will remain with the school **[Ap] [An]**

However, TADS does not have reliable profits and Ollie invested all of his savings into the business **[Ap]**, meaning a permanent increase in the hourly rate for all teachers would raise fixed costs **[K]*** *and could cause further financial difficulty **[An]**

TADS should choose an increase in the hourly rate **[E]**. Since TADS's goal is specifically to retain its current teachers** [Ap]**, a higher hourly rate directly rewards all staff for their existing contribution to the school** [An]**. Commission only benefits teachers who recruit new pupils and does not address the needs of those with a full timetable, making an hourly rate increase the more effective and fair solution for improving teacher retention **[E]**
